transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-20 15:00 PDT
Duration: 47 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Sofia Tran (Redwood AE), Marcus Lee (Redwood SE), Tom Alvarez (Orchid VP Eng), Lisa Chen (Orchid ML Eng), Raj Patel (Orchid SRE)

Summary (auto): Quick hosted API demo focusing on chat/text generation basics: streaming, request params (temperature/top_p/max_tokens), and retry patterns. Discussed latency vs cost, caching, kv cache, and security (SOC2/SAML/KMS). Agreed to pilot and benchmarks.

Topics:
- Hosted API overview and console walkthrough
- Streaming responses and SDK examples
- Parameter tuning (temperature, top_p, max_tokens, stop)
- Retries, idempotency, and backoff patterns
- Batching, prefix caching / KV cache and cost tradeoffs
- Security: SOC2, SSO/SAML, KMS, VPC peering options

Transcript:
[00:00] Sofia: Hey everyone, thanks for taking the time, quick intro — I'm Sofia from Redwood, joined by Marcus on the SE side.
[00:12] Tom: Hey Sofia, thanks. I'm Tom, VP Eng, with Lisa and Raj. We're mainly evaluating hosted first, maybe Dedicated later.
[00:20] Sofia: Great, we'll run through the hosted API demo — show chat generation, streaming, params, and then Marcus will go deeper into retries and perf.
[00:30] Marcus: Quick note, if anything is noisy, just interrupt. We'll try to keep examples practical.
[00:41] Lisa: Our main goals are sub-300ms p50 for short messages, p95 under 800ms, and cost per active session under $0.10/day. Also SSO and logs for audits.
[00:56] Marcus: Good, helps to know targets. Hosted can meet those for many workloads; we'll map model selection + batching to cost/latency.
[01:10] Sofia: Opening the Console — here's the model catalog, curated open models, and our Redwood-verified performance profiles. You can pin a model version and enable streaming in the route settings.
[01:30] Sofia: Demo: hitting the hosted chat endpoint via the SDK, streaming enabled. I'll start a request that streams tokens to the client.
[01:45] (screen share noise)
[01:53] Marcus: Note — streaming is chunked over SSE or websocket depending on SDK. In Node we use the streaming client to append tokens as they arrive, so UI feels responsive.
[02:10] Lisa: Is there a sample for incremental rendering? We have a React front end.
[02:17] Marcus: Yes — I'll share the React streaming example (we put it in the repo). It's basically client.on('token') append. Also shows how to cancel or call stop sequences.
[02:34] Tom: About parameters — what do you recommend for temp/top_p/max_tokens for transactional chat?
[02:40] Sofia: For transactional short replies, temp 0.0–0.4, top_p 0.8–0.95; max_tokens keep tight e.g., 60–150. For creative, raise temp. We also support stop sequences to truncate.
[02:58] Marcus: And we expose sampling params in the request object so you can A/B them per route. Also per-route quotas and rate limits in the console.
[03:14] Lisa: Cost control — curious about batching and prefix caching, you mentioned kv cache during onboarding?
[03:21] Marcus: Right — Redwood runtime does automatic prefix / KV caching for repeated system prompts or context. That can drop per-token compute. Batching is workload-aware — but for sub-300ms p50 you might configure smaller batches for latency-sensitive routes.
[03:40] Tom: If we use hosted, what are fallback behaviors if capacity is constrained?
[03:47] Sofia: We do smart routing by policy: latency-first routes prefer lower-latency variants, cost-first can route to smaller quantized models. We also have automatic fallback to compatible model variants and queued bursts, depending on plan.
[04:04] Raj: For security, we need SOC2, SAML SSO, and KMS for keys. Also audit logs retained 12 months.
[04:12] Sofia: We have SOC2 Type II, SSO via SAML/OIDC, and KMS integrations for private deployments; hosted supports customer-managed keys via our enterprise package. Audit logs can be exported to your SIEM. I'll send the compliance pack.
[04:30] Lisa: Do you offer VPC peering or private connectivity?
[04:34] Marcus: Yes — Hosted customers can use private peering options for Dedicated; for fully private we offer Redwood Private (VPC/on-prem). For the initial pilot hosted with peering often suffices.
[04:50] Tom: Let's talk about retries — we saw spikes in latency in our testing with other vendors. What's best practice?
[04:58] Marcus: Use idempotency keys for create-like calls. For streaming, you generally retry at request-level when you get network errors, with exponential backoff and jitter. We recommend a 3-retry default with exponential backoff, and client-side hedging for p95-sensitive routes. We'll share concrete SDK examples.
[05:20] Marcus: Also set a per-request timeout and use early-abort signals in the SDK to avoid duplicate work. For non-streaming generation, you can also enable server-side retries with idempotency to avoid double tokens being charged.
[05:40] Lisa: Do tokens charged on partial stream? How do billing semantics work with retries?
[05:46] Sofia: Billing is per-token accepted by the runtime; if a retry causes duplicate generation we have safeguards — on enterprise plans we can reconcile duplicates, but client-side idempotency is the recommended path. We'll document edge cases in the pricing doc.
[06:05] Tom: For benchmarking, what metrics should we capture?
[06:10] Marcus: p50/p95 latency, token throughput, tokens-per-dollar, and cache hit rate. Also trace correlation IDs so you can map a request through our traces. Our console exposes per-route breakdowns by token, latency, cost.
[06:28] (short silence, typing)
[06:40] Sofia: Quick demo of parameter tuning — changing temperature from 0.2 to 0.8 in the console live, you can compare outputs and save a model config.
[06:58] Lisa: Nice — can we lock config per environment? Prod vs staging?
[07:03] Sofia: Yes, you can set per-route configs and pin model versions. Also rollouts — canary and A/B tests supported from the Console.
[07:20] Tom: Any limits on streaming throughput for hosted?
[07:25] Marcus: Depends on plan. Hosted standard has soft limits; Dedicated reserves GPU pools for throughput guarantees. For your QPS targets you may start hosted and move to Dedicated when you hit predictable loads.
[07:42] Raj: About data retention — if we send PII, is it stored?
[07:48] Sofia: By default we retain logs minimally for monitoring; enterprise options include no retention or customer-managed retention policies. For regulated data we recommend Private or Dedicated with customer controls.
[08:02] Lisa: For our pilot we want a one-week trial with a small test set and a benchmark run. What do you need?
[08:08] Marcus: We'll need sample prompts, expected session lengths, and target qps. We'll run the benchmark with your dataset, show p50/p95, and recommend model/quantization profiles.
[08:20] Tom: Can you run quantized model suggestions? We want to see 4-bit profiles for cost savings.
[08:24] Marcus: Yes — Redwood Optimize will recommend quantization and batching settings for cost/perf tradeoffs. We'll include suggested configs in the bench report.
[08:40] Sofia: I'll put together pricing and the security pack. Marcus will run the bench with your inputs.
[08:46] Lisa: On retries again — do you expose circuit-breaker metrics?
[08:50] Marcus: Console shows error rates and retries, and you can set alerts on regression in quality or latency. We also surface per-route retry counts.
[09:05] (scene: demo moves back to code snippets)
[09:15] Marcus: Here is a Node snippet for streaming and retries: set timeout, attach token handler, set idempotency-key header for create, and exponential backoff on network failures. I'll share exact code in the repo link.
[09:35] Tom: We'll need language-specific examples — we use Go on the backend and React on the frontend.
[09:41] Marcus: We have Go + Python + Node SDKs; React example is in the examples folder.
[09:50] Lisa: Anything we should watch for in long chat histories — memory growth or token limits?
[09:55] Marcus: Use prefix caching for repeated system prompts and summarize long histories into condensed context to stay within token windows. We support KV cache to persist commonly used history chunks.
[10:12] Raj: For observability, is there tracing wrap?
[10:16] Sofia: Yes, tracing hooks and per-request trace IDs are in the console; you can export logs to your SIEM.
[10:25] Tom: Ok great. Any gotchas switching from other vendors?
[10:30] Marcus: Mostly mapping rate limits and retry semantics; also watch tokenization differences across models which can affect costs. We provide tokenizer tools to estimate token counts.
[10:45] Lisa: Walkthrough of how to enable streaming via the console route settings?
[10:50] Sofia: Sure — open Route > Edit > Streaming toggle > pick model and sampling params > Save. Then you can test in the built-in playground.
[11:08] (shared test request, short stream sample)
[11:20] Marcus: For rollback and rollouts we recommend canary at 5–10% then monitor errors. Console has automatic fallback policies if canary fails.
[11:34] Tom: We'll probably want a small canary first.
[11:38] Sofia: Recap: We'll send pricing + security pack, Marcus shares SDK + streaming/retry examples, customer to send test prompts and expected QPS, schedule benchmark with SRE.
[11:52] Raj: I'll coordinate infra details for peering and egress.
[11:57] Lisa: And we'll run initial integration on staging.
[12:05] Sofia: Great — thanks everyone. We'll follow up on the thread.
